content: In the circulatory system, veins are blood vessels responsible for transporting blood back to the heart. Most veins carry deoxygenated blood from the tissues to the heart, with the exception of the pulmonary and umbilical veins, which carry oxygenated blood. Veins are tubular structures that collapse when their lumens are not filled with blood. The outermost layer of a vein is composed of collagen and is wrapped in bands of smooth muscle, while the interior is lined with endothelial cells. Many veins are equipped with one-way valves, known as venous valves, which prevent the backflow and pooling of blood, particularly in the lower extremities, where gravity exerts its effects. The anatomical location of veins varies significantly between individuals, more so than arteries. The total capacity of veins is sufficient to hold the entire blood volume of the body. This capacity is regulated by the venous tone of the smooth muscles, which reduces the cross-sectional area and volume of individual veins, thereby minimizing the total volume of the venous system. Helical bands of smooth muscle surrounding veins assist in maintaining blood flow to the right atrium of the heart. In cases of vasovagal syncope, the relaxation of these smooth muscles causes blood to pool in the veins of the lower extremities, reducing the return of blood to the heart and brain, which can result in fainting. Veins play a critical role in returning blood from organs to the heart. In systemic circulation, oxygenated blood is pumped by the left ventricle through arteries to the body’s muscles and organs. At the capillaries, nutrients and gases are exchanged, and the blood, now deoxygenated and carrying cellular waste and carbon dioxide, enters the veins. This deoxygenated blood is transported to the right atrium, then to the right ventricle, and subsequently pumped to the lungs via the pulmonary arteries for reoxygenation. In pulmonary circulation, oxygenated blood is returned to the left atrium by the pulmonary veins, completing the cycle of blood circulation. The skeletal-muscle pump aids in the return of blood to the heart, counteracting the low blood pressure in the venous system. Prolonged standing can lead to blood pooling in the legs, causing insufficient blood return to the heart and potentially resulting in fainting. Neurogenic and hypovolemic shock can also cause fainting due to the relaxation of smooth muscles around veins, leading to blood pooling and reduced cerebral perfusion. While it is commonly stated that arteries carry oxygenated blood and veins carry deoxygenated blood, this is an oversimplification. All veins carry some oxygenated blood, though the oxygen content is typically much lower than that of arterial blood. Medically, veins are frequently accessed for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. Venipuncture allows for the withdrawal of blood specimens for testing, while intravenous delivery enables the infusion of fluids, electrolytes, nutrients, and medications. Intravenous delivery can be performed via syringe injection or catheter insertion. Peripheral veins, such as those in the hand or arm, are commonly used for catheter placement. However, for highly concentrated or irritating substances, central veins may be accessed, sometimes requiring catheter insertion into the superior vena cava. For long-term use, a more permanent access point may be surgically created. The most common venous disorder is venous insufficiency, which often manifests as spider veins or varicose veins. Treatment options vary based on the type and pattern of the veins and the physician’s preferences. These treatments may include radiofrequency ablation, vein stripping, ambulatory phlebectomy, foam sclerotherapy, sclerotherapy, laser therapy, or compression therapy. Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is a condition in which a blood clot forms in a deep vein, potentially leading to pulmonary embolism and chronic venous insufficiency. Phlebology is the medical specialty dedicated to diagnosing and treating venous disorders. Diagnostic techniques include patient history, physical examination, venous imaging, and laboratory evaluation for venous thromboembolism. The American Medical Association recognizes phlebology as a self-designated practice specialty. Notable veins include the pulmonary veins, which carry oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart, and the superior and inferior venae cavae, which transport deoxygenated blood from the upper and lower systemic circulations, respectively. Portal venous systems, such as the hepatic portal vein and hypophyseal portal system, connect two capillary beds directly. The blood in veins appears dark red due to its high carbon dioxide content, in contrast to the bright red arterial blood rich in oxygen. Veins appear blue through the skin because subcutaneous fat absorbs lower-frequency light, allowing only higher-energy blue wavelengths to penetrate and reflect off the dark veins. This phenomenon, known as Rayleigh scattering, is also observed in the blue iris of the eye. Veins can be classified into several categories: portal versus non-portal veins, superficial versus deep veins, and pulmonary veins versus systemic veins.
